items.comment: Wiktionary treats дідусь as the diminutive or affectionate form of дід, which is closer to "grandpa" but also used as the everyday word. "grandfather" is acceptable.

Goroh gives ону́ка (animate, feminine, 1st declension). English Wiktionary gives ону́ка [oˈnukɐ], "granddaughter", with вну́ка as an alternative form. Goroh's definition page and slovnyk.ua (СУМ) cross-refer онука to внука, defined on Goroh as "Дочка сина або дочки". Standard Ukrainian and not a Russian form; unlike онучка, it showed no foot-wrap homonym in the entries I read.

JIPA gives /a/; Vakulenko's Table 1 gives [ɑ] when stressed and [ɐ] when unstressed or after palatalised consonants. Father fits [ɑ] and is acceptable as an approximation. The а in авто́бус is unstressed, so the example is not the clearest model of this comparison.

items.note: голова́: head. A voiced fricative, partner of х. Phoneticians describe it differently: /ɦ/ in the published IPA illustration, [ʕ] or [ɣ] in Vakulenko 2025. English h is closer to х. The sound of g has its own letter, ґ.
items.comment: Checked against both papers. /ɦ/ matches JIPA's table. Vakulenko gives ʕ before а, о, у, и, е and ɣ before voiced consonants and word-finally, says [ɦ] lacks convincing experimental confirmation, and concludes English [h] is phonetically close to Ukrainian [x], so the note reports him accurately. "English h is closer to х" rests on Vakulenko alone; JIPA does not address it. The note omits his possible plosive allophone [g], and JIPA's [x] before /k/; neither omission misleads at this level.

items.note: ґа́нок: porch. A rare letter, but easy to confuse with г.

items.comment: The clue fits the phoneme, but JIPA's own transcription of the example is дім [dʲim], so it has a palatalised д, not the plain sound of dog. I passed it because the clue makes no claim that contradicts this, unlike the dark-l clue for л, and the difference is small for an English speaker. Vakulenko also treats plain д as dental (d̪), a difference small enough to fall within the unit's stated approximation.

/jɛ/ is correct for this example, at the start of a word. After a consonant є marks softness rather than a separate [j] (JIPA p. 352), which the cell does not say. An omission, not an error. The same applies to ю and я.

/j/ could be misread by an English speaker as the j of jam, but "as in boy" and the example йо́гурт resolve that. Both contexts match JIPA p. 352: й stands for /j/ only syllable-finally, as [i̯], or before о.

As with д: the clue fits the phoneme, but Wiktionary gives the example ніч as [nʲitʃ] with a palatalised н, and Wikipedia gives ні as /nʲi/. I passed it because the clue makes no claim that contradicts this, unlike the clue for л.

/x/ is in both papers. Many English speakers pronounce loch with [k], so the comparison only helps those who know the Scots sound, but it is the closest available and the unit calls comparisons approximate.

/ʃt͡ʃ/ matches JIPA p. 353, which adds that it can reduce to [t͡ʃ] or [ʃ]. JIPA's narrow transcription shows this very word що reduced in running speech (ʃə, t͡ʃə), with ʃt͡ʃɔ in the broad transcription. The clue gives the careful form, which is right for a learner.

items.comment: /ju/ is correct for this example, at the start of a word. After a consonant ю marks softness (JIPA: люк [lʲuk]), which the cell does not say. An omission, not an error.

/ja/ is correct for this example, at the start of a word. After a consonant я marks softness (JIPA: ряд [rʲad]), which the cell does not say. An omission, not an error. Vakulenko's [ɐ] after palatalised consonants does not affect this example.

items.note: вода́: water. It varies by position: labiodental [ʋ] before front vowels, nearer [w] before rounded back vowels, and [u̯] at the end of a syllable, as in був (was, masculine). Vakulenko 2025 disputes [w], since the lips barely protrude, and writes [β̞].
items.comment: All claims check out. JIPA p. 352 gives [ʋ] before front vowels, [w] before rounded back [u ɔ] and [u̯] syllable-finally; був is ˈbuu̯ in JIPA and masculine past "was" per Goroh and Wiktionary. Vakulenko does call the w label an error, reports the lips barely protruding, and writes β̞ (code points match his text). His case also rests on F2, which the note omits, and his Table 2 gives β̞ for the syllable-final ў too, so his dispute reaches [u̯] as well as [w]. Neither omission misleads a learner.

items.note: ла́мпа: lamp, with the hard [ɫ]. Before і it is soft: лі́то (summer) has [lʲ].
items.comment: ла́мпа verified: Goroh and Wiktionary give ла́мпа, feminine, "lamp", and Wiktionary gives [ˈɫampɐ]. лі́то is [ˈlʲitɔ] (Wiktionary). This resolves my earlier flag on this cell. "Before і it is soft" is slightly absolute: Wikipedia, Ukrainian phonology, says consonants are typically palatalised before /i/ and that non-palatalisation is rare but allowed. Acceptable at this level. "hard" and "soft" match JIPA p. 352's usage.

items.note: о́ко: eye. Unlike Russian, it does not reduce towards a without stress: вода́ is never вада́. It can still shift slightly, towards [o] before a stressed /u/. Vakulenko 2025 describes the vowel as close-mid [o] rather than /ɔ/.
items.comment: All claims check out, and this resolves my earlier flag on this cell. Russian merges unstressed /o/ with /a/ (Wikipedia, Russian phonology; Wiktionary has Russian вода́ as [vɐˈda] and Ukrainian as [wɔˈda]). The shift to [o] before stressed /u/ is in JIPA p. 354. Vakulenko does describe /о/ as close-mid [o], always above the midline. The note names one shift only; Vakulenko's rise in F2 for unstressed /о/ and JIPA's general reduction in fluent speech go unmentioned, but "can still shift" does not exclude them. The clue is unchanged and acceptable as before.

items.note: ри́ба: fish. Retracted and lowered compared with і. Close to the Russian vowel [ɨ], but not the same sound. Vakulenko 2025 transcribes it as a lowered, advanced [ɨ] instead.
items.comment: The meaning holds after the rewording, and "Russian vowel [ɨ]" is now JIPA's own term (p. 353: "phonetically different from Russian [ɨ]"). It is also slightly more accurate, because Russian [ɨ] is written ы and also и after ж, ш, ц (Wikipedia, Russian phonology). The judgement call from my last check stands: "not the same sound" is well supported, but "close to" has only indirect support (Vakulenko's barred [ɨ] symbol, и replacing ы in Russian loanwords, informal commentary), with no acoustic comparison found and nothing contradicting it. Passed as an approximation. "instead" means instead of /ɪ/, a minor ambiguity because it follows the [ɨ] sentence.
